message.abstract: <jats:sec><jats:title>Background</jats:title><jats:p>Prophylactic antibiotics are traditionally given as a single dose for caesarean section. However, inconsistent application of recommendations and recent evidence prompted a literature review.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Objectives</jats:title><jats:p>To assess the optimal regimen for antibiotic prophylaxis in caesarean section by comparing single versus multiple doses of the same intervention.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Search strategy</jats:title><jats:p><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MEDLINE</jats:styled-content>, Web of Knowledge, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">SCOPUS</jats:styled-content>,<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"> CENTRAL</jats:styled-content> and ongoing trials databases were searched. Reference lists were reviewed and international groups contacted.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Selection criteria</jats:title><jats:p>Randomised controlled trials (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RCT</jats:styled-content>) comparing single with multiple dose regimens of the same antibiotic prophylaxis. Quasi‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RCT</jats:styled-content> and abstracts were suitable for inclusion.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Data collection and analysis</jats:title><jats:p>Reviewers independently extracted data and assessed quality of evidence. A random‐effects model was used and results presented as risk ratio (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content>) with 95% confidence intervals (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content>).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Main results</jats:title><jats:p>Sixteen studies were included, involving 2695 women. Nonsignificant differences were observed between single dose and multiple dose antibiotic prophylaxis in the incidence of postpartum infectious morbidity (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> 0.95, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.75–1.20, <jats:italic>I</jats:italic><jats:sup>2</jats:sup> = 25%), endometritis (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> 1.03, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.74–1.42, <jats:italic>I</jats:italic><jats:sup>2</jats:sup> = 0%) and wound infection (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> 1.22, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.72–2.08, <jats:italic>I</jats:italic><jats:sup>2</jats:sup> = 0%). A trend towards lower risk of urinary tract infection was seen with multiple dose (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RR</jats:styled-content> 0.65, 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content> 0.34–1.24, <jats:italic>I</jats:italic><jats:sup>2</jats:sup> = 0%).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title><jats:p>There was insufficient evidence to determine whether there is a difference between single and multiple dose regimens in reducing the incidence of infectious morbidity after caesarean section. The quality of evidence was very low and well‐designed <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RCT</jats:styled-content>s are needed.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Tweetable abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Insufficient evidence of difference between dosage regimens of antibiotic prophylaxis in caesarean section.</jats:p></jats:sec>
title: Single dose versus multiple dose of antibiotic prophylaxis in caesarean section: a systematic review and meta‐analysis
